title: Exploring a sustainable building's impact on occupant mental health and cognitive function in a virtual environment
target_construct: Assessing built environment impact on occupant cognitive function and mental health using neurophysiological data

findings.antecedent: Sustainable building (SB) environments (compared to Conventional building (CB) environments)
findings.consequent: Visual system engagement (measured by bilateral occipital region activity, theta/delta increases, alpha decreases)
findings.source: Abstract, Results and findings: CB versus SB, Discussion and conclusion
findings.validation_evidence: Overall, the recorded data provided evidence supporting differences between SB and CB features. For hypothesis 1, test subjects demonstrated increased visual system engagement in the SB compared to that in the CB.

statistics.details: Still Images (0-500 ms): significantly greater activity in bilateral occipital regions (associated with processing visual information) (p<0.01, uncorrected Wilcoxon nonparametric comparisons, Fig 6 topo maps). Occipital processing increases for the SB, relative to the CB, are readily apparent for each band in the 0–500 ms range (delta, theta, and alpha). Decreases in alpha for SB (blue color, for SB-CB, i.e., greater alpha amplitude for the CB) areas were associated with increased occipital processing for the SB. Still Images (500-1000 ms): Increase in occipital processing is sustained in the 500-1000 ms range only for alpha. Video: Significant increases in theta band activity in the SB, including medial-frontal, centroparietal, and occipital areas. Delta and theta evidenced substantially more significant increases (red lines) for the SB relative to the CB, while alpha evidenced substantially more significant decreases (blue lines) for the SB relative to the CB.

findings.antecedent: Sustainable building (SB) environments (compared to Conventional building (CB) environments)
findings.consequent: Attentional focus and control processing (measured by frontal region activity, theta increases, alpha increases, frontal connectivity decreases)
findings.source: Abstract, Results and findings: CB versus SB, Discussion and conclusion
findings.validation_evidence: For hypothesis 2, test subjects exhibited increased modulated attentional focus and control processing in the SB compared to that in the CB.

statistics.details: Still Images (0-500 ms): Broad decreases in frontal regions (associated with control processing, problem-solving, movement, and social interaction). Broad and bilateral increases in frontal alpha were observed in the 0-500 ms range. Decreased connectivity within frontal regions (p<0.05, uncorrected, Fig 6). Still Images (500-1000 ms): Broad and bilateral increases in frontal alpha... continuing through 500-1000 ms, with bias towards the left side. Relatively localized increases in lateral-frontal areas can be observed in the theta band, where hypotheses predicted modulated engagement of lateral prefrontal areas associated with control. Video: Significant increases in theta band activity in the SB, including medial-frontal, centroparietal, and occipital areas. Delta and theta evidenced substantially more significant increases (red lines) for the SB relative to the CB, while alpha evidenced substantially more significant decreases (blue lines) for the SB relative to the CB.

findings.antecedent: Combined virtual environment (VE) and EEG/ERP approach
findings.consequent: Ability to provide objective neurophysiological information about built environment impact on affective and cognitive functioning
findings.source: Abstract, Discussion and conclusion, Limitations and next steps
findings.validation_evidence: The present study provides initial validation of the proposed approach... The core approach provided robust differences between SB and CB virtual environments, with readily interpretable findings (e.g., mindfulness), providing validation that the proposed cognitive-neuroscience/virtual-design approach can index important differences in the occupant experience of the built environment.

findings.consequent: Shift towards a more active and engaged mental stance, greater focus on the present environment, reduced internal mental processing (mindfulness), lower extrinsic cognitive load
findings.source: Abstract, Discussion and conclusion, Cognitive-load processing modulated by SBs
findings.validation_evidence: Initial findings suggest that SB built environments may encourage a shift, consistent with mindfulness... The present findings can be explained by the cognitive load theory, which is consistent with the interpretation of greater focus on the present environment and reduced internal mental processing (cf. mindfulness), based on the observed increased theta/delta activities and greater engagement of visual systems and corresponding decreases in frontal activity in the SB environment. Reflected as less mind wandering, in an SB environment, the extrinsic cognitive load is lower, which gives the brain more power to process the intrinsic load.

statistics.details: Based on observed increased theta/delta activities and greater engagement of visual systems and corresponding decreases in frontal activity in the SB environment.

findings.antecedent: Increased occupant mindfulness in SB environments
findings.consequent: Stronger environmental satisfaction and support, positive association with job satisfaction, better performance, and well-being of residents
findings.validation_evidence: The idea of increased occupant mindfulness as a mechanism is consistent with the reports that occupants in SB environments feel stronger environmental satisfaction and support. Physical workplace satisfaction has been positively associated with job satisfaction and better performance, and environmental satisfaction has been linked to contributions to the well-being of residents, particularly the elderly.

components.name: Virtual Environment Immersion
components.description: Presents built environment stimuli (lighting, view, spatial quality) to participants in a simulated virtual building.
components.validation: Demonstrated clear differences in how subjects responded to different environments and to still images versus a more realistic three-dimensional environment (video).

components.name: Electroencephalogram (EEG) device
components.description: Measures brain activity (visual system, cognitive system responses) during VE immersion, including time-frequency amplitude and phase-synchrony (functional connectivity).
components.validation: Used to collect data that showed robust differences between SB and CB environments, providing objective neurophysiological information.

components.name: Event-Related Potential (ERP) approaches
components.description: Analyzes EEG data to identify brain activity in response to specific events (stimuli) within the built environment.
components.validation: Used to decompose activity, differentiate theta (3-7 Hz) and delta (0-3 Hz) contributions, and measure functional connectivity (TF interchannel phase synchrony).

components.name: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT)
components.description: Theoretical framework used to interpret the impact of physical built environment characteristics (volume, density, lighting, spatial arrangement, presence of others) on cognitive load (intrinsic and extrinsic) and subsequent behavior/cognitive function.
components.validation: Findings are consistent with interpretations based on CLT, linking observed brain activity to concepts like reduced mind-wandering and lower extrinsic cognitive load.

psychometric_properties.validity: Initial validation of the proposed approach, showing robust differences between SB and CB virtual environments with readily interpretable findings (e.g., mindfulness), indicating the approach can index important differences in occupant experience.

recommended_use: To advance design methods by soliciting occupants' neurophysiological responses prior to project completion; to provide a cost-effective approach for parameterizing beneficial SB features and manipulating identified features in proposed built environments before costly construction; to enable designers to change designs based on neuroscience responses to identify optimized design solutions.
limitations: Building parameters (lighting, spatial dimensions, nature views) were assessed together, making it difficult to isolate the effects of individual parameters.
Different types of spaces (e.g., private vs. public) were assessed together, limiting inferences about specific space types.
Only one primary built environment was assessed, making it difficult to infer which manipulated parameters are more general versus specific.
Only short-term effects were measured in the virtual environment, and it is unknown if these are representative of long-term real-world impacts.

paper_metadata.title: Exploring a sustainable building’s impact on occupant mental health and cognitive function in a virtual environment
paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Exploring a sustainable building’s impact on occupant mental health and cognitive function in a virtual environment
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractEven though people spend the majority of their time indoors, the role of buildings in shaping human experience is still not well understood. The objective of this experimental project is to develop, test, and validate a data-driven neuroscience approach to understand the built environment’s impact on occupant cognitive function and mental health. The present study utilized virtual environments and electroencephalogram (EEG) and event-related potential (ERP) approaches, to provide objective neurophysiological information about how sustainable buildings (SBs) impact people’s affective and cognitive functioning differently compared to conventional building (CBs). The long-term goal is to assess the validity of sustainable building design protocols in promoting and increasing mental health and well-being and the mechanism used to accomplish these increases. The findings showed test subjects demonstrated increased visual system engagement and modulated attentional focus and control processing in the SB compared to the CB environments. The findings can be explained by the cognitive load theory, which is consistent with the interpretation of greater focus on the present environment and reduced internal mental processing (cf. mindfulness), based on the observed increased theta/delta activities and greater engagement of visual systems and corresponding decreases in frontal activity in the SB environment. In addition, the combination of virtual environment (VE) and EEG/ERP has the potential to advance design methods by soliciting occupants’ responses prior to completion of the projects. Building design is more than aesthetics; expanding the horizon for neuroscience would eventually result in a new knowledge base for building design, particularly sustainable building design, since the sustainability of the building often needs to be quantified.
